part_title: SageMaker Neo, Unified Studio and ML Pipelines

scenes.title: Compile for Target Hardware with Neo
scenes.narration: SageMaker Neo is illustrated as a model compilation step. On the left, a trained model from a supported framework is provided alongside a target-device specification. The compiler in the centre optimizes that model for compatible hardware and supported operators. On the right, the compiled artifact can be deployed into a suitable cloud, container or edge runtime. Notice the compatibility note at the bottom: optimization depends on framework version, model operations and target hardware. Compiling an artifact does not mean every model can run on every device. Validate numerical accuracy, model size, execution latency and required runtime dependencies on actual target hardware. The key takeaway is that deployment performance can depend on compilation and device compatibility, not only the model's parameters. Check current service support before choosing Neo for a new architecture.

scenes.title: Deploy a Compiled Model at the Edge
scenes.narration: This slide follows a four-stage edge deployment path. First, a supported model is compiled for the target using SageMaker Neo. Second, the optimized artifact is stored in S3 and packaged with the necessary inference runtime as an AWS IoT Greengrass component. Third, that component is deployed to compatible edge devices. Fourth, predictions run locally on those devices without needing a network round trip for every inference request. The architecture diagram moves from trained model to compiler, S3, Greengrass and an edge endpoint. Local inference can reduce latency and limit data transfer, but only if the package fits the device's memory, compute and security constraints. Device rollout, updates and rollback remain operational responsibilities. A compiled model file alone is not a complete fleet-management strategy.

scenes.title: Collaborate in SageMaker Unified Studio
scenes.narration: This slide maps a shared SageMaker Unified Studio workspace. Data scientists, machine-learning engineers, data engineers and analysts enter through a common domain, where permissions and governance apply. Inside the domain, a project groups the team, its resources and work on a particular use case. Notice the four areas in the project: shared data and assets, collaborative notebooks, model development and pipelines. The right-hand cards describe benefits such as discovering authorized datasets, collaborating in the same development environment and sharing reproducible workflows. The distinction between a domain and a project matters. The domain establishes broader governance and access, while projects organize specific teamwork. Even in a unified interface, individuals should receive only the permissions necessary for their tasks. Use these boundaries to keep experimentation productive without allowing every user unrestricted access to datasets and deployment systems.

scenes.title: A Unified Studio Project Journey
scenes.narration: This numbered diagram takes us from idea to a repeatable machine-learning workflow. Step one creates or selects a project within the domain. Step two connects approved data sources and sets up access. Step three develops and trains in a notebook, using shared tools and kernels where appropriate. Step four tracks model versions and artifacts so experiments are reproducible. Step five orchestrates processing, training and evaluation in a pipeline. Step six brings the team together to inspect results, review feedback and decide the next experiment. Follow the orange loop at the bottom labelled iterate and improve. A unified workspace helps make all six activities visible, but it does not remove testing, approval or access controls. Preserve the identities of datasets and model versions so a final deployed model can be linked back to the work that produced it.

scenes.title: Orchestrate with SageMaker Pipelines
scenes.narration: This final slide is an example of a directed machine-learning pipeline. A processing step first ingests and transforms data. A training step builds the model. An evaluation step then tests quality on a held-out dataset. Look at the decision diamond in the middle: if the metric meets the approved threshold, the workflow registers the model as a candidate in Model Registry. If the metric fails, the pipeline stops rather than registering an unsuitable version. The lower row emphasizes reusable executions and lineage. Each pipeline run records artifacts, parameters, metrics and relationships, helping with repeatable experiments and audit. A registered model may still require a separate approval before production deployment. The reason to use pipelines is to automate predictable, testable operations while preserving quality gates, traceability and the ability to iterate. That completes our SageMaker lifecycle module.
